sum: Walt Disney (NYSE: DIS) will publish fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year results before regular trading on Tuesday, followed by an 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time webcast, according to its investor announcement. The report will provide the next official assessment of operating performance; the partnership announced this week does not itself establish an earnings benefit.

The shares traded at $119.07 at 3:25 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 13, up $0.84, or 0.71%, from $118.23. Stock Analysis labels the dollar quote real-time. It is an intraday reference, not a closing price. Research for this report was completed on November 14 in Tbilisi, while the U.S. trading date remained November 13.

Disney and Adobe (Nasdaq: ADBE) announced their multiyear alliance on November 9. Adobe will provide early access to creative and AI technologies, including Firefly, Firefly Foundry, Premiere and Photoshop, alongside engineering and research support.

The work spans Disney’s production pipeline, StudioLAB and ESPN Edge. Adobe said co-innovation projects were already underway. The announcement did not quantify contract value, cost savings or incremental profit, leaving investors without a basis for adding a specific financial contribution to forecasts.

The potential attraction is practical: tools that accelerate concept development could improve how creative teams work. That is an analytical possibility, rather than a disclosed earnings result. Implementation costs, the usefulness of outputs and the protection of creative works will help determine the commercial return.

Disney’s August 5 SEC-filed earnings release reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $25.248 billion, compared with $23.650 billion a year earlier. Entertainment operating income rose to $1.680 billion from $1.022 billion.

But nine-month operating cash flow fell to $12.515 billion from $13.627 billion. Investment in parks, resorts and other property rose to $6.780 billion, leaving non-GAAP free cash flow of $5.735 billion, down from $7.519 billion.

Is Adobe Stock’s Fall A Bargain Or A Warning?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Adobe (ADBE) stock closed at $236.70 on November 10, 2026, finishing 12.5% below its October 22 high. Declines of this size tempt buyers to step in because they make a profitable software company cheaper. But the same drop can also mark the beginning of a deeper slide. So has buying Adobe after its sharp falls paid off before?

Buying Adobe after a sharp fall has paid off only half the time. Since 2010, the stock has dropped more than 20% within 30 trading days 12 times, and 10 of those falls are now more than a year old. Five of the 10 left the shares higher a year later, and the median result was a 2.5% loss. The most recent falls that can be judged went against buyers: the three in 2024 and 2025 were each lower a year later, by 21% to 35%, while the two in 2026 are too recent to judge.

Buyers also sat through further losses along the way. In the median case, the lowest close during the year after a fall was 17.1% below the price on the day of the drop. The highest close took a median of 168 days, or about five and a half months, to arrive.

The business under the stock is growing faster than it was a year ago. Adobe’s revenue rose 12.9% in the quarter that ended August 28, 2026, against 10.7% growth in the same quarter of 2025. Adobe also turns a large share of its sales into cash: operations brought in $10.8 billion over the past twelve months, 41.6% of revenue. New users keep arriving: management said on the September 10 call that monthly users among business professionals and consumers grew more than 25% from a year earlier, to over 900 million, and that monthly users of the Acrobat AI assistant doubled from the quarter before.

On profit, Adobe is cheap against the market. Adobe now trades at 12.8 times its earnings over the past twelve months, against 22.3 times for the S&P 500. At the end of September, Adobe’s P/E was lower than at every quarter end of the past ten years but one, in June 2026.

The soft spot is revenue Adobe has signed but not yet booked. Management said on the September 10 call that this contracted revenue grew 8% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026, trailing the 13% rise in sales.

Adobe stock faces a December test after Citi growth warning
sum: Adobe is heading into its next earnings report with a stronger operating base but a more demanding growth debate. In an analysis published by Yahoo Finance on Thursday, November 5, the focus was on Citi's November 4 downgrade, Adobe's valuation and the company's ability to sustain growth as artificial intelligence tools challenge established software products.

Citi cut Adobe to Sell from Hold and lowered its price target to 207 US dollars from 250 US dollars. Analyst Tyler Radke expects a weaker fiscal 2027 outlook when Adobe reports its fiscal fourth-quarter results. The bank reduced its estimate for net new annual recurring revenue to 1.5 billion US dollars in fiscal 2027 and 1.45 billion US dollars in fiscal 2028, cuts of 470 million and 500 million US dollars, respectively.

The upcoming forecast will be delivered during a management transition. Anil Chakravarthy is scheduled to become chief executive officer on December 1, while Shantanu Narayen is set to become executive chair. David Wadhwani is leaving his role overseeing Adobe's creativity and productivity business, and Steve Day is serving as interim chief financial officer.

Citi also sees pressure from Adobe's shift toward user acquisition and lower-priced offerings rather than relying primarily on price increases. The bank expects artificial intelligence-native and web-based competitors, weaker small-business demand and unmonetized AI inference costs to weigh on growth and margins. For investors, the key issue is whether a broader user funnel can eventually offset slower monetization per customer.

Adobe's fiscal third quarter ended August 28 with record revenue of 6.76 billion US dollars, up 13 percent from the prior-year quarter. Total annualized recurring revenue increased 11.2 percent to 27.50 billion US dollars, while non-GAAP earnings per share rose 15 percent to 6.13 US dollars. Management raised its full-year non-GAAP earnings-per-share target to a range of 24.45 to 24.50 US dollars.

The analysis also highlighted Adobe's cash generation and share repurchases as support for earnings per share. The company repurchased about 9.5 million shares in the third quarter, and its share count fell from 413 million to 391 million during the first nine months of fiscal 2026.

Citi cuts Adobe rating on ’rising risk of a hard reset’
sum: Investing.com -- Citi downgraded Adobe to Sell, saying it sees downside risk to consensus growth estimates into fiscal 2027 as a leadership transition coincides with mounting competitive and macro pressure on the company's Creative business.
"[We] see rising risk of a hard reset," the bank's analysts said, cutting their price target on the stock to $207 from $250.
Adobe shares fell more than 2% in premarket trading Wednesday.

Citi said incoming CEO Anil Chakravarthy, who takes over Dec. 1, assumes the role "amid key leadership vacancies," including the CFO and the head of Digital Media. Given those gaps and the Creative unit's evolving go-to-market strategy, the bank expects a weaker fiscal 2027 outlook when Adobe reports fourth-quarter results in early December.

"A "hard reset" would pressure shares near term but provide time to rebuild leadership, refine strategy, and establish a more achievable base to accelerate," Citi analysts wrote. They expect the new CEO to make "thoughtful, strategic changes" to Creative, potentially at the expense of near-term growth.

Adobe's recent results and industry data suggest competitive, AI and macro and small-business pressures are intensifying, the analysts noted. The team expects Adobe to lean more on top-of-funnel growth through AI and Firefly, rather than on its classic Creative Cloud suite, which has relied on price increases.

That shift in focus to monthly active users will likely weigh on total annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027 and 2028, Citi said, as Adobe continues to forgo price-increase-driven monetization and steers new users toward lower-priced offerings. The impact should be greatest in core Creative, compounded by weak small-business demand and competition from web-based and AI-native tools.

items.t: AI doesn’t destroy art but raises the bar for even better content creation, says Adobe APAC chief
sum: These common mistakes are fuelling negative sentiment about AI among the creative community, with many perceiving the drastically increased accessibility to graphic design and content creation more as a bane than a boon.
Not only is AI taking away their jobs, many have said, but it is also destroying the intrinsic value of art.
But Adobe, the world’s largest provider of creative software, believes AI can play a dominant role in the future of content creation without harming the industry.

The flood of AI content will only make audiences more discerning, and that only increases demand for quality content, says Ben Goodman, president of Asia-Pacific and Japan (JAPAC) at Adobe, in an interview with The Straits Times.
“There was definitely a period of time when AI increased the volume of content and created a bifurcation in the market,” Goodman says.
“People very quickly began to understand content that was created by AI no longer met their standards, and that raised the bar for content.”
With more people now able to create content, audiences’ expectations and standards have also been raised.

Borsa Italiana: tax incentives to encourage greater investment in shares
sum: Savings accounts with low minimum withdrawal thresholds, extension of the IPO bonus, tax relief for recapitalisations: proposals from Assonime and the Stock Exchange

In recent years, there has been a surge in efforts by institutions and market participants to revitalise the capital market. There has been the manifesto for the development of the capital market in Italia, initiatives such as the fund of funds – managed by CDP – aimed at listed SMEs, regulatory simplifications and the reform of the Consolidated Law on Finance (TUF); yet new listings on the Milan Stock Exchange remain scarce and savers are still investing far too little in shares. Direct investment in shares by Italian households, as a percentage of GDP, is in fact among the lowest in Europe, whilst, by contrast, investment in bonds – particularly government bonds – is much higher than elsewhere.

Assonime (the association of public limited companies) and Borsa Italiana have therefore set to work to try to draw up a series of concrete proposals to ensure that resources and the real economy find common ground on the stock market, with a view to guiding the behaviour of savers and businesses, which is currently heavily influenced by a culture of debt – a practice that, incidentally, enjoys tax incentives. For this reason, the proposals drawn up focus on tax matters, in the hope that they may be incorporated into a forthcoming budget bill, sooner rather than later.

The highlight of the proposals is the savings and investment accounts, which have been the subject of an EU Recommendation (SIA, i.e. Savings & investments accounts) and are therefore the subject of debate in all Member States wishing to follow the Swedish example: by introducing this type of tax-advantaged account, Sweden has, over the course of some fifteen years, made investing in shares almost as popular as investing in government bonds here in Italy.

The Assonime-Borsa study suggests two approaches to tax treatment. The simplest involves applying a minimum tax (set at 0.7 per cent per annum) on the average value of the investment, which would allow all other forms of taxation to be avoided, for example on capital gains or dividends, whilst also exempting the accounts from inheritance tax, as is already the case today for BoT and BTp.

Adobe Jumps 5% as Beaten-Down Software Names Rebound Despite Risk-Off Day; Salesforce Rises 3%
sum: Enterprise software stocks are staging a surprise rebound even as large-cap tech crumbles around them, and the reason buyers are zeroing in on Adobe and Salesforce reveals a sharp divide in how Wall Street now thinks about AI risk.

Beaten-down enterprise software leaders are drawing buyers even as large-cap tech sells off, a selective bounce that favors names hit by artificial intelligence (AI) fears. Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE | ADBE Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $268.31, a move that puts the creative software maker at the front of the sector rebound. Meanwhile, Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) stock is up 3% to $248.81, trailing the rally in Adobe shares while still climbing against the tech selloff.

Large-cap tech is under heavy pressure, with the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) down 3%. Software stocks as a group are barely moving, as the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (CBOE:IGV) is down 0.2%. Buyers are singling out Adobe and Salesforce while the broader group stalls.

Each company serves a different buyer: Adobe offers subscription creative and document tools, while Salesforce sells customer relationship software to businesses. Both businesses rely on recurring subscription sales, so fears that AI tools could replace parts of customer workflows have weighed on Adobe and Salesforce shares this year, and generative image and video tools sit closest to Adobe’s creative lineup, which puts the company at the center of that debate.

Adobe’s partner NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) expanded its collaboration with the creative software maker on October 15 to speed up AI features in Photoshop and Premiere on the chipmaker’s hardware. The tie-up lands on the central worry for Adobe shares, which have lagged this year as investors weigh whether AI tools threaten the company’s creative software business. Quicker generative features inside core apps give Adobe a concrete way to argue that AI increases customer reliance on its tools.

This bounce offers Adobe holders relief after a year in which the market treated the company as a likely AI casualty, yet a single partnership announcement doesn’t settle whether creators keep paying for premium subscriptions as cheaper AI tools spread. Skeptics can argue the rebound in Adobe shares still needs fresh evidence of customer demand to last.

sum: Net profit below consensus. The advertising business remains robust, but there is growing pressure on profitability and free cash flow. The share price is up in after-hours trading

Meta has published its quarterly results. Zuckerberg’s group – regarding which, just before the financial results were released, news broke of a multi-billion-dollar fine in the US for privacy breaches, has recorded a turnover of 64.601 billion dollars. This figure represents a 26 per cent increase compared with the same period in 2025. As for operating profit, Meta recorded a figure of 12.988 billion, down 37 per cent. Finally, net profit stood at 9.860 billion, more than tripling the figure from a year earlier. However, this figure did not exceed estimates.

With regard to operating costs and expenses, however, Meta recorded 51.61 billion, up 68 per cent compared with the same period last year. This increase, which was also influenced by legal costs, highlights growing pressure on the group’s cost structure. At the same time, capital expenditure (CapEx) totalled $34.91 billion, reflecting the intensification of financial efforts directed towards the development of technological infrastructure. Despite this, the company continued to reward shareholders through the distribution of dividends totalling $1.36 billion. As at 30 September 2026, cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities totalled $82.45 billion, confirming a strong liquidity position.

Operating cash flow stood at 32.79 billion. However, the high level of investment resulted in a negative free cash flow of 2.12 billion dollars. This divergence between operating cash generation and residual liquidity highlights how infrastructure expansion is absorbing an increasing share of the resources generated. Today, however, the first things investors think about are Canva, Figma, and the growing number of AI tools that can generate images and videos from a simple text prompt.
The real question facing Adobe is therefore not whether its revenue can grow next quarter.
When AI allows almost anyone to create images, videos, and designs, will people still need Adobe?

My view is that the market’s concerns are not unreasonable. However, Adobe’s current share price appears to be pricing in an extremely pessimistic outcome: not only that Adobe will lose its growth, but that it may gradually lose its pricing power across the entire creative software market.

sum: I have spent the last few days poring over the data, the charts, and the endless debates surrounding Adobe, and I have come to a conclusion that might sound contrarian given the market's mood: 2025 was a massive setup. We are looking at a company that is undeniably a big part of the software industry, yet it is being treated like a relic that is about to be wiped off the map by artificial intelligence. When I look at the actual numbers rather than the scary headlines, I see a disconnect that offers a rare opportunity. The market has put Adobe in the penalty box, pricing it as if its growth story is over, but the underlying fundamentals tell a completely different story of resilience, massive profitability, and a strategic pivot that is far more successful than the share price suggests.

I am looking at a company that just delivered double-digit revenue growth, expanded its margins to levels that are the envy of the sector, and bought back a staggering amount of its own stock. Yet, the stock price has spent much of the last 12 months drifting lower, down significantly from its highs. This divergence between financial performance and market sentiment is where I find value. The prevailing narrative is that generative AI is an existential threat that will shrink Adobe's user base. However, my analysis suggests that Adobe is successfully transitioning from a defensive incumbent to an offensive AI platform. With a valuation that has compressed to near-historic lows relative to its peers, I believe the downside is capped by its massive cash flows, while the upside from a narrative shift could be substantial.

For those who might only know Adobe as the company behind PDF files, it is worth resetting the baseline on what this machine actually does. Adobe operates primarily in digital media and digital experience. It provides the essential software tools for creative professionals; photographers, video editors, graphic designers; as well as marketing and document solutions for enterprises. Its products like Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, and Acrobat are standard industry requirements. The business model has largely shifted to subscriptions, creating a highly recurring revenue stream that has historically commanded a premium valuation.

items.t: Challenger cuts Pepper Money bid amid deteriorating share price
sum: Challenger has reduced its bid for non-bank lender Pepper Money, citing ‘deteriorating market conditions’.

The firm had stated in early February that it had been “engaging in discussions relating to a potential transaction” around acquiring Pepper Money. Discussions were “advanced” and it had been granted exclusive due diligence but there was no certainty it will result in an offer.
However, on 17 March, Challenger stated it had reduced the offer from $2.60 per share to $2.25 per share, a 13 per cent reduction.

“Under the revised proposal, Challenger has reduced the offer price from $2.60 per share to $2.25 per share, less the final fully franked Pepper Money 2025 dividend of 7.8 cents per Pepper Money share and any special dividend. The revised proposal represents Challenger’s best and final offer, in the absence of a superior proposal.
“The discussions remain incomplete and there is no certainty that the Revised Proposal will eventuate in a transaction.”
A subsequent ASX announcement from Pepper Money stated the decision by Challenger to reduce the bid had been made due to “the deterioration in both market conditions and the operating environment”.
Shares in Pepper Money have declined 9.8 per cent over the past month although they are up by 50 per cent over one year to 17 March.

sum: Shares of creative software giant Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) fell 3.1% in the afternoon session after the "AI replacement" narrative reached a fever pitch following the release of new models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

The simultaneous debut of Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 and OpenAI's "Frontier" agent platform raised concerns that autonomous agents are no longer just tools, but new operating systems that can cannibalize traditional software. This suggests that specialized applications might be reduced to mere features within frontier models, rendering legacy seat-based licensing models increasingly obsolete.The catalyst is the models' unprecedented agentic power. Opus 4.6's "software hunting" capability allows it to autonomously audit and patch complex codebases, while OpenAI's Frontier platform bypasses traditional CRM and ticketing interfaces to perform enterprise work directly. By commoditizing sophisticated workflows into low-cost API calls, these releases threaten the recurring revenue of software giants. As AI builds bespoke tools on demand, the market is aggressively repricing the entire software application layer.

sum: Software stocks are in a freefall. Adobe stock price continued its freefall this week, reaching its lowest level since April 2020. It has now erased all the gains made during the pandemic, while its market capitalization has plunged from $350 billion to $107 billion today.

Other software companies are in a freefall too. ServiceNow’s stock price crashed to $109 on Tuesday, down from the all-time high of $239, while Microsoft has plunged to $411 from the record high of $553.
Other top companies in the software industry, like Intuit, LegalZoom, and Atlassian, have all continued their strong downward trend this year.

As a result, the closely-watched iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) plunged to $85 from its all-time high of $117. Its biggest constituent companies are Microsoft, Palantir, Salesforce, Oracle, Intuit, AppLovin, Adobe, and Palo Alto Networks.

There are three main reasons why these software stocks have imploded this year. The most important one is that there is the ongoing fear that these companies will be disrupted by AI tools, especially those made by Anthropic.
For example, companies like LegalZoom and Thomson Reuters plunged on Tuesday after Anthropic released a new tool to automate legal work, including contract reviewing and legal briefings.

Other software companies plunged after the company launched Claude Cowork tool, which can automate most tasks done by companies. The fear is that AI will disrupt these industries as tools get more advanced.

Thanksgiving turkey 101: How to safely thaw a frozen turkey
sum: We're just a few days out from Thanksgiving, and it's time to talk turkey.

Anyone gearing up to cook the centerpiece poultry for the moveable feast has likely already ordered or is planning to pick up their turkey soon, so if you're starting from frozen, here's what you need to know to properly thaw out your bird.
There are three methods to safely thaw a turkey: in the refrigerator, in cold water and in a microwave oven.

Thawing it out in the fridge is the recommended option by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, because the turkey can defrost at a consistent temperature, which prevents the possible growth of harmful bacteria.
The fridge method can take a bit longer -- a full 24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds.

On average, a Thanksgiving bird that feeds four to six people is about 11 pounds or more, so consider working backwards on the timing for your prep and recipe when using this method, because based on the size, it could take a few days before the turkey is ready to cook.
When thawing in the fridge, leave the turkey in its wrapping and place it on the bottom shelf on a large sheet tray or pan that can catch any excess liquid.

For Software Stocks, It’s Been an AI Bust, Not a Boom
sum: - Software stocks have lagged AI names by a significant margin for most of 2025.
- Software stocks are significantly undervalued, according to Morningstar analysts, and many have sound fundamentals despite recent declines.
- Morningstar analyst Dan Romanoff points to ServiceNow as an attractive buy.

Excitement around artificial intelligence has propelled many technology stocks to record heights, except for one notable group: software. In fact, many of the biggest software stocks are posting significant losses for the year. And by Morningstar equity analysts’ metrics, some look like bargains.

Driving the losses is a persistent fear that AI will upend the software industry, either by reducing licensing revenue by making it easier and less labor-intensive to perform tasks without human input or by rendering traditional software applications totally obsolete. “There is a lot of concern,” says Morningstar senior equity research analyst Dan Romanoff. “No one really knows how this is going to play out.”

Combine this with the fact that software firms are generating little revenue from AI, a changing forecast for interest rate cuts, and long-tail slowdowns after the covid-era software boom, and you have a recipe for a “brutal” selloff that has accelerated since July and intensified over this past week as the tech sector fell. A side effect of those losses has been a steep drop in valuations, with major software names like ServiceNow NOW, Salesforce CRM, and Adobe ADBE trading at discounts of 20% or more.

With several quarters of strong earnings in the books, Romanoff says there’s plenty of upside to be found. While a pandemic-driven surge in revenue has faded, software stocks regularly beat the S&P 500 Index in terms of revenue growth. “They offer a lot of attractive elements to me that haven’t really changed all that much,” he says, even amid new advancements in AI.
